title: Classical polynomial-time integer factorization and discrete logarithms

concept.text: The innovation would be a classical algorithm, or complementary algorithms, that can factor general integers and solve specified discrete-logarithm problems with a proved running time polynomial in the input bit length, while remaining practical at cryptographic sizes. Factoring means recovering an integer’s prime factors. A discrete logarithm means recovering the exponent that produces a given group element from a specified base. These computations underpin important public-key cryptographic systems.

For the concrete scope developed here, the discrete-logarithm target is prime fields, including cryptographically difficult prime-order subgroups. Discrete logarithms in other finite fields, on elliptic curves, or in more general represented groups would require explicitly stated additional coverage. A solution for prime fields would not by itself establish a solution for elliptic curves.

Proposed interpretation: the breakthrough combines a mathematical guarantee with usable computation. A polynomial bound with an enormous exponent or constant could be theoretically important without enabling practical cryptanalysis. Conversely, an impressive isolated computation would demonstrate performance on that input without proving polynomial scaling. The intended innovation requires both general algorithmic scope and convincing practical performance.

significance.text: Practical classical factoring and prime-field discrete logarithms would fundamentally change algorithmic number theory and the security assumptions behind RSA, finite-field Diffie–Hellman, and finite-field DSA. Factoring an RSA modulus enables private-key recovery; solving the relevant discrete logarithms enables recovery of finite-field Diffie–Hellman secrets and attacks on discrete-logarithm-based signatures. The significance is conditional on the proposed capability becoming practical at the parameter sizes used by the affected systems.

Recorded communications could become readable where the retained protocol data and key-establishment mechanism permit reconstruction of the necessary secrets. This consequence depends on the particular protocol and available records. Elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman would also be threatened if the breakthrough separately solved elliptic-curve discrete logarithms. Neither that extension nor routine execution on ordinary computers follows from a successful prime-field computation on a classical cluster.

The impact would have an important boundary: cryptographic systems rely on different mathematical assumptions. NIST’s ML-KEM standard, published on 13 August 2024, relates its security to Module Learning with Errors. A factoring or discrete-logarithm algorithm alone would therefore not establish an ML-KEM break. Equally, this distinction cannot guarantee that every lattice scheme would survive every new mathematical technique associated with the breakthrough.

Efficient quantum factoring supplies a comparison with a different computational model. A practical classical algorithm would make the attack possible without the fault-tolerant quantum machine assumed by quantum resource estimates. The quantum path still involves substantial implementation requirements, explicit algorithmic assumptions, and unfinished analyses in the cited estimate, so describing its remaining obstacles solely as engineering would be too strong.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a general classical method with a proved polynomial bound in input bit length for factoring and the stated prime-field discrete-logarithm problem. The number-field sieve provides the documented baseline. Its familiar complexity estimate has the form exp(c(log N)^(1/3)(log log N)^(2/3)(1+o(1))) for problem size N and an appropriate constant c. Relative to an input length proportional to log N, this grows faster than any fixed polynomial but more slowly than an exponential in that length. This is a heuristic complexity estimate, not a proved general polynomial bound, and the 2020 paper emphasizes its limited numerical precision.

The scientific barrier is to replace that scaling with a rigorously justified general algorithm. Faster implementations, better sieving, and new size records can improve practical performance without supplying this missing guarantee. The documented computations also show why the engineering side matters: hundreds or thousands of core-years at roughly 800 bits do not establish feasible execution at 2048 bits.

Proposed requirements for resolving the remaining barriers include controlling polynomial exponents and constants, memory consumption, preprocessing costs, and parallel resource use. A discrete-logarithm method must also handle genuinely difficult subgroup parameters rather than derive its apparent success from specially easy instances. If elliptic curves or broader group families are included, the algorithm and proof must establish that broader scope separately.

The supplied evidence establishes the historical baseline and the proposed target, but it does not establish a comprehensive absence of classical polynomial-time algorithms through 1 November 2026. It also does not determine the largest cryptographically relevant quantum execution by that date. Those limits constrain claims about the latest state of the field; they do not turn the proposed classical capability into an achieved result.

current_state.text: Boudot and coauthors’ Crypto 2020 paper reports the factorization of RSA-240, a 795-bit integer, and a discrete-logarithm computation over a 795-bit prime field. It also reports the factorization of RSA-250; its 829-bit size follows from the displayed modulus. These are concrete classical computational achievements in the supplied evidence.

The paper reports 953 reference core-years for RSA-240 and 3177 reference core-years for DLP-240, using the same reference hardware for that comparison, and roughly 2700 core-years for RSA-250. Core-years measure accumulated computational effort rather than elapsed wall-clock duration. These results support a comparison between factoring and prime-field discrete logarithms at the investigated sizes; they do not establish a corresponding elliptic-curve result or routine 2048-bit computation. The paper also provides a companion code repository as a basis for reproducing its work.

RSA-250 is the largest factored RSA challenge modulus documented in the supplied reviewed source set. Its standing as a global record on 1 November 2026 remains unverified because the supplied freshness record is empty. The research mentions alleged September 2026 secondary reports of an RSA-260 factorization, but supplies no supporting report or published method. That allegation remains unsubstantiated here; the evidence gap does not establish that it is false. The supplied sources likewise do not establish the largest hardware execution of Shor’s algorithm, so a current toy-only limit cannot be asserted from this record.

Craig Gidney’s arXiv preprint dated 21 May 2025 estimates that a 2048-bit RSA integer could be factored in less than a week with fewer than one million noisy qubits. This is a conditional quantum resource estimate, not a completed factorization or a classical algorithm. Its assumptions include a 0.1% gate error rate, a one-microsecond surface-code cycle, a ten-microsecond reaction time, specified connectivity, and algorithmic assumptions. The paper leaves detailed cold-storage analysis and simulations under different workloads to future work. The supplied record does not establish subsequent peer-reviewed publication.

These descriptions rely on the supplied review’s document assessment. For the Boudot paper, the review had a full 30-page PDF text extraction in addition to HTML that omitted figure contents and the full numerical table; the reported costs and challenge outputs were available in the PDF prose. Gidney’s PDF text was available in full, but figure graphics were not inspected. The FIPS 203 extraction was truncated on page 56, while its relevant abstract and MLWE discussion were present. These access limits permit the specific textual conclusions used here without implying a complete visual examination of the documents.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mathematical demonstration: publish a refereed classical algorithm, or algorithms, with an explicit proved bound polynomial in input bit length for general integer factorization and prime-field discrete logarithms. The specification should state the supported input families, correctness guarantees, and any randomization or success-probability assumptions. The proof must establish the claimed general scope; finite computational tests establish demonstrated breadth, not literal universality or asymptotic complexity.
completion_criteria.label: Proved classical polynomial-time general factoring and prime-field discrete logarithms

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical demonstration: factor a previously unfactored RSA modulus of at least 2048 bits and compute a discrete logarithm in a prime field of comparable modulus bit length with a cryptographically substantial prime-order subgroup. Use documented classical hardware and report the software, inputs, outputs, elapsed runtime, total processor effort, memory requirements, preprocessing, and verification data. Independent reproduction and runs across varied inputs would strengthen confidence in correctness and practical breadth. The 2048-bit threshold and these reporting requirements are proposed criteria, not established community standards.
completion_criteria.label: Classical ≥2048-bit RSA factoring and comparable prime-field logarithms with documented resources

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: measure performance across increasing input sizes to expose large constants, high polynomial degrees, and resource bottlenecks. Account for any preprocessing and clarify whether it is reusable across targets. A cluster demonstration would establish practicality on that documented system; claims about ordinary computers would require corresponding evidence. Elliptic-curve discrete logarithms would require a separate proof and demonstration if added to the scope.
completion_criteria.label: Measured resource scaling across input sizes, including preprocessing costs

completion_criteria.text: The 2020 computation’s companion code repository supplies a relevant reproducibility precedent. A larger number-field-sieve record would remain a valuable achievement but would not, by itself, establish polynomial classical complexity. Similarly, a quantum resource estimate or quantum execution would not satisfy the classical objective.
completion_criteria.label: Number-field-sieve records and quantum results do not establish classical polynomial-time complexity

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MAT-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems, shares the aim of making difficult computations practical through polynomial algorithms. MAT-06 targets particular arithmetic problems. Success on these targets alone would not establish practical algorithms for NP-complete problems generally, so the entries remain distinct.

MAT-09, Classical polynomial-time algorithms for cryptographic lattice problems, is the closest cryptographic neighbor in the supplied roster. Its title identifies a separate family of computational targets. FIPS 203 provides a concrete example of this distinction through ML-KEM’s reliance on Module Learning with Errors. The supplied material contains no fuller MAT-09 specification, so its exact coverage cannot be inferred, and neither entry should be merged into the other.

Roster-based synthesis: MAT-02, An effective global Langlands correspondence over number fields, shares a broad number-theoretic setting with MAT-06, but its title supplies no demonstrated reduction to practical factoring or discrete logarithms. MAT-05, Research-scale machine-checked mathematical discovery, could potentially assist with discovering or verifying an algorithm and its proof; it concerns a method of mathematical research rather than this particular computational capability.

Roster-based synthesis: MAT-04, Proved polynomial-cost solution of high-dimensional nonlinear PDEs, and MAT-08, Polynomial-time chemical accuracy for molecular electronic structure, share MAT-06’s concern with rigorous scaling and useful numerical performance, while addressing different problem classes. MAT-03, A first-principles theory of turbulent transport, and MAT-07, A prescriptive mathematical theory of deep learning, seek predictive or prescriptive theories in other domains. The supplied roster establishes no direct technical dependency between those entries and MAT-06.

Quantum factoring is a useful external comparison because it addresses the same factoring target with different computational resources. It does not fulfill MAT-06’s classical requirement. Likewise, finite-field and elliptic-curve discrete logarithms must remain distinguishable: the reviewed classical experiments concern prime fields, and their results do not establish an elliptic-curve algorithm.

unresolved_issues: The latest state of classical polynomial-time factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms through 1 November 2026 is not established by the supplied freshness record.
The alleged September 2026 RSA-260 reports, their methods, and their validity remain unverified; RSA-250’s global record standing at the as-of date is likewise unresolved.
The largest hardware execution of Shor’s algorithm and whether any cryptographically relevant execution occurred by the as-of date are not established here.
The title leaves open whether eventual scope should extend beyond prime fields to broader finite fields, elliptic curves, or general represented groups.

The supplied record does not establish subsequent peer-reviewed publication or experimental realization of Gidney’s 2025 preprint estimate; its stated assumptions and unfinished analyses remain material.
Only MAT-09’s title is supplied, so its detailed relationship to particular lattice problems and schemes cannot be resolved.
The BSD comparison and exact BQP statement lack dedicated support in the supplied evidence and have not been independently resolved.

brief.title: Fast solutions to the maths behind encryption
possible: The secrets behind some encrypted communications could become recoverable without quantum hardware. Computers could efficiently factor large numbers, meaning find their prime factors, and solve discrete logarithms, meaning recover the exponent used to produce a given answer.

The logarithm method would cover prime fields: arithmetic using remainders after division by a prime, including hard cryptographic cases. Both methods would have proved polynomial running time: time bounded by a fixed power of input length. They would also work practically at cryptographic sizes.
why: Security systems based on these problems would need replacement. These include RSA encryption and signatures, alongside prime-field Diffie–Hellman for establishing shared secrets and DSA for digital signatures.
This would change algorithmic number theory and make these attacks possible without building a quantum computer.

milestones.label: General methods with proved polynomial running time
milestones.explanation: Peer-reviewed proofs would have to establish general classical methods for factoring and prime-field logarithms, with explicit correctness guarantees. This would establish the mathematical capability beyond individual successful computations.

milestones.label: Practical attacks at cryptographic sizes
milestones.explanation: A demonstration would factor a previously unfactored RSA number of at least 2048 bits and solve a comparably sized prime-field logarithm with a hard subgroup and documented resources. This would establish practical performance.

milestones.label: Measured costs across increasing input sizes
milestones.explanation: Runs across growing inputs would have to measure time, memory and advance preparation, including whether that preparation can be reused. This would reveal costs that could make a mathematically efficient method impractical.

milestones.label: Evidence that establishes the classical scaling claim
milestones.explanation: The result would need evidence of classical polynomial scaling beyond larger computations with existing methods or quantum results. Those achievements alone cannot establish the required classical guarantee.

uncertain: The proposed practical size threshold is a judging criterion, rather than an established community standard.
The acceptable running time, memory use and role of randomized success guarantees still need precise targets.
Extending the target to elliptic curves, another mathematical setting used in cryptography, would require separate proofs and demonstrations.

page.title: Classical polynomial-time factoring and prime-field discrete logs
page.definition: Classical, non-quantum algorithms factor arbitrary integers into primes and recover discrete logarithms—exponents x from g and g^x modulo a prime—including in subgroups formed by powers of g. Each algorithm has a proved running time polynomial in input bit length; zero-error randomized algorithms may use polynomial expected time.

goal.need: NIST's 2020 comparison assigns 112-bit security strength to a 2048-bit RSA modulus and to finite-field systems with a 2048-bit modulus and 224-bit subgroup order. Classical polynomial-time algorithms would undermine the corresponding computational hardness assumptions. Their execution cost at these finite sizes would still depend on the polynomial's constants and degree.

completion.title: Both target problems have proved classical algorithms with polynomial bit complexity.
completion.criterion: A peer-reviewed proof establishes uniform classical algorithms that factor every integer N ≥ 2 completely and, for every prime p, base g of supplied order q, and h in its subgroup, return x with 0 ≤ x < q and g^x ≡ h modulo p. Each algorithm has a proved O(b^k) bit-operation bound, for total input length b and a fixed k: worst-case time if deterministic, or expected time with zero error if randomized. The bound includes preprocessing and makes no unproved number-theoretic assumptions.
completion.set_by: Cryptographic community convention, explicitly stated by RSA Laboratories in FAQ v4.0, Question 2.3.9; polynomial and randomized complexity conventions follow Handbook of Applied Cryptography, §2.3.
completion.threshold_quote: a ‘breakthrough’ means finding a polynomial time algorithm.
completion.basis: RSA Laboratories explicitly identifies polynomial time as the breakthrough criterion for the two problems. The Handbook distinguishes polynomial complexity from performance at particular input sizes. This mathematical test supplies no additional wall-clock, memory or hardware requirement.

milestones.title: Classical algorithms run in polynomial time when relevant prime factors are polynomial in input bit length.
milestones.criterion: For input bit length b and any fixed c, trial division, primality testing and perfect-power handling factor N when its second-largest distinct prime divisor is at most b^c. For prime-field logarithms, Pohlig–Hellman with baby-step–giant-step takes polynomial time when every prime divisor of the supplied group order q is at most b^c; q can then be factored by trial division. Gaudry's §§1.2–1.3 establish these restricted families.
milestones.set_by: Algorithmic-number-theory convention documented by Gaudry, CIRM 2014, §§1.2–1.3. The quotation states the factoring condition; Theorem 4 and its following complexity analysis supply the logarithm condition.
milestones.threshold_quote: factoring integers N for which the second largest prime is bounded by a polynomial in log N can be done in polynomial time.

milestones.title: A classical computation solves the published 795-bit benchmark for a target problem.
milestones.criterion: Factor the single RSA-240 challenge modulus, or solve the single DLP-240 target in Appendix A: modulus p = RSA-240 + 49204 and base 5, with p and (p−1)/2 prime. Boudot and colleagues report both results in 2020. For the factoring case, Lu's developer report records RSA-260 factors obtained on 3 September 2026 using a GPU implementation of the general number field sieve; that report is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Computational benchmark convention: RSA Laboratories' RSA-240 challenge and Boudot and colleagues' DLP-240 challenge, specified and solved in their CRYPTO 2020 paper.
milestones.threshold_quote: the factorization of RSA-240, a 795-bit number, and a discrete logarithm computation over a 795-bit prime field.

milestones.title: At least one target problem has a proved classical polynomial-time algorithm.
milestones.criterion: An unconditional classical polynomial-time algorithm solves every valid input of either complete problem class, using the correctness and complexity conventions specified in completion. Establishing this result for one case leaves the other case required for joint completion.
milestones.set_by: RSA Laboratories, FAQ v4.0, Question 2.3.9, applies its polynomial-time breakthrough criterion to factoring and discrete logarithms individually.
